About

I study economics at Stanford and co‑founded Verdnt Group.

Next summer I’ll join DRW’s central strategy team in Chicago.

I’m also interested in computer science and philosophy, and I like understanding what people value and how they put ideas to use.

Building

Verdnt Group

I co-founded Verdnt Group. We’re building Verdnt Studio, a tool for food and drink teams developing new drinks. The goal is to help them turn market research into product ideas they can test.

Co-founder

More on Verdnt Studio

Verdnt Studio pulls its research from social media and retail shelves. I work with clients to understand what they need and build the software.

Our client work includes software that combines market research with a company’s product information to suggest new products. Teams can check the sources behind each suggestion before deciding what to test.

Trus

I co-founded Trus to help people create software for their own work. The idea was to describe what you needed and have AI build a workspace for it. Trus is now retired.

Co-founder · Retired

How Trus worked

I helped build the first version, where AI assembled workspaces from a set of tables, charts, calendars, and other components we had built.

I later focused on product direction and finding customers, while Diego led the engineering.

Values

Optimization

I look for the one change that makes the biggest difference. When I coached karate, I filmed my students’ sparring rounds and watched them technique by technique, looking for the one thing to fix. I go through a spreadsheet or a team’s workflow the same way.

From: coaching at Okaigan Karate, and client work

Human relations

The people close to me come first. Cutting hair taught me how much a half hour of real conversation is worth: I started in high school and ended up with more than fifty regulars. My favorite thing to do on campus is still to catch up with a friend over a haircut.

From: cutting hair since high school

Multiplying throughput

I would rather build something that does a job every time than do it once by hand. I run a small team of AI agents that handle my coding and notes: they take the routine steps, and I keep the calls that need judgment. At Morgan Stanley I built agentic workflows for portfolio monitoring and client data tracking.

From: my agent setup and Morgan Stanley, 2026

Candor

I want a straight answer, including when something failed or an idea isn’t worth doing, and I try to give one back.

From: how I work with teammates and my agents

Books

Books I’ve read and still think about, and some suggested reads. Pick a book off the shelf to see its cover and a note.

Read

Suggested reads

My Brilliant FriendElena Ferrante

My Brilliant Friend

Elena Ferrante

Elena and Lila have no family or legal tie, and they keep choosing to stay friends. Ferrante gives a lot of weight to what they leave unsaid.

My favorite novel

Diagnostic Political PhilosophyHans Sluga

Diagnostic Political Philosophy

Hans Sluga

Sluga asks how to make good decisions without the full picture, especially in politics with a lot of misinformation around. Economics raised the same question for me.

I helped research and edit it

Beyond Good and EvilFriedrich Nietzsche

Beyond Good and Evil

Friedrich Nietzsche

I read it in weekly meetings across a desk from Professor Sluga. He always had another question, so I made sure I’d done the reading before I came in.

Read with Hans Sluga

The Order of ThingsMichel Foucault

The Order of Things

Michel Foucault

I helped build more than 200 pages of material for Sluga’s graduate seminar on it. I broke hard ideas into steps a graduate student could follow.

Seminar material

The Tyranny of MeritMichael J. Sandel

The Tyranny of Merit

Michael J. Sandel

I read them side by side for a Stanford writing class, and I still don’t know what merit should be. In all three, institutions keep changing what counts as merit, and the definition decides who wins. Kirn also writes about the gap between performing competence and having it.

One of three books on meritocracy

Good Strategy/Bad StrategyRichard Rumelt

Good Strategy/Bad Strategy

Richard Rumelt

Rumelt argues that a good strategy names the real problem, picks an approach to it, and lines up actions behind that approach.

Start here for consulting and product work, especially when a plan is full of vague business language.

About the book
The Sciences of the ArtificialHerbert A. Simon

The Sciences of the Artificial

Herbert A. Simon

Simon writes about designed systems and how they fit their environment, and about deciding with limited information.

Economics and AI both come up, through the question of how to design things.

About the book
Thinking in SystemsDonella H. Meadows

Thinking in Systems

Donella H. Meadows

A short introduction to stocks, flows, feedback loops and delays, and what happens when you change a system.

A data pipeline changes how people work and what they get rewarded for, and this book helps you think that through.

About the book
The Beginning of InfinityDavid Deutsch

The Beginning of Infinity

David Deutsch

Deutsch argues that knowledge grows through explanation and criticism, and that progress could keep going.

The account of how knowledge improves fits practical work as well as philosophy.

About the book
7 PowersHamilton Helmer

7 Powers

Hamilton Helmer

Helmer describes seven conditions that let a business keep an advantage that competitors can’t copy.

Use it to ask what would stop competitors from copying an AI product or services business.

About the book
High Output ManagementAndrew S. Grove

High Output Management

Andrew S. Grove

Grove explains how a manager measures output, sets up processes, runs meetings and develops people.

A founder taking on more projects and more people will get the most from it.

About the book
The Mom TestRob Fitzpatrick

The Mom Test

Rob Fitzpatrick

A short guide to asking customers about their past behavior, since people tend to be polite about your idea.

Read it before any customer interview, for product or consulting work.

About the book
The Effective ExecutivePeter F. Drucker

The Effective Executive

Peter F. Drucker

Drucker covers how executives spend their time, set priorities, use their strengths and make decisions.

The advice on getting useful work done fits most business and product jobs.

About the book
Seeing Like a StateJames C. Scott

Seeing Like a State

James C. Scott

Scott looks at large planning schemes that forced simple administrative models onto complicated local life.

Keep it in mind on any automation project that might ignore how people on the ground do the work.

About the book
Finite and Infinite GamesJames P. Carse

Finite and Infinite Games

James P. Carse

Carse separates games played to win from games played to keep the game going.

It raises the question of which business goals are worth chasing. It’s written in short aphorisms.

About the book
AntifragileNassim Nicholas Taleb

Antifragile

Nassim Nicholas Taleb

Taleb writes about systems that get stronger from shocks, and argues for keeping options open and limiting the downside.

Its ideas fit running experiments well. The big claims deserve some skepticism.

About the book
The Nicomachean EthicsAristotle

The Nicomachean Ethics

Aristotle

Aristotle on living well, virtue, friendship and practical judgment.

Aristotle treats character as something you build by practicing, which fits a discipline like karate.

About the book
Zero to OnePeter Thiel with Blake Masters

Zero to One

Peter Thiel with Blake Masters

Thiel argues that startups should build something new.

Check its strongest claims against real customers and market data before acting on them.

About the book
The Innovator’s DilemmaClayton M. Christensen

The Innovator’s Dilemma

Clayton M. Christensen

Christensen explains why well-run incumbents can lose ground when disruptive technologies arrive.

It helps explain how incumbents adopt AI. The strategy books in higher tiers are more practical.

About the book
The Structure of Scientific RevolutionsThomas S. Kuhn

The Structure of Scientific Revolutions

Thomas S. Kuhn

Kuhn describes normal science, the anomalies it can’t explain, and how scientific paradigms change.

Some of it carries over to how technology changes, though science and startups only compare so far.

About the book
MeditationsMarcus Aurelius

Meditations

Marcus Aurelius

Marcus Aurelius’s private Stoic notes on judgment, duty, how nothing lasts, and how to act.

Read it for discipline and staying calm. The short entries are easy to reread.

About the book
On LibertyJohn Stuart Mill

On Liberty

John Stuart Mill

Mill argues for individual freedom and open debate, and for limits on how far society can interfere with a person.

It’s about thinking and writing for yourself, and it leaves room to question how the principles work inside institutions and online.

About the book
Reasons and PersonsDerek Parfit

Reasons and Persons

Derek Parfit

Long, detailed arguments about rationality, personal identity, morality and what we owe people over time.

It’s dense and slow to get through alongside other projects. That time is why it sits in C tier.

About the book
The Sovereignty of GoodIris Murdoch

The Sovereignty of Good

Iris Murdoch

Three essays on goodness, on how we see other people, and on the limits of ethics built around the will.

There’s little direct business advice in it.

About the book
The GoalEliyahu M. Goldratt with Jeff Cox

The Goal

Eliyahu M. Goldratt with Jeff Cox

A business novel about a manufacturing plant’s problems that explains the theory of constraints.

The bottleneck ideas apply directly to operations. The story takes longer to read than a short summary of the theory would.

About the book
